<description>
The C++ Core Guidelines recommend **establishing an error handling strategy early in a project's design** ([E.1](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#re-design)). Under the presumption that "we are still early" and given the fact that there is lots of development (eg #34931, #35003, #34132, ...) without such a strategy, it might be the right time to come up with a design document.

I post this as a PR rather than an Issue, because it will simplify giving feedback on individual parts of the text.
</description>

[2026-10-07] c:6043494977 comment by stickies-v (member):
Concept ACK on documenting error handling guidelines, so they can be used to avoid repeating the same discussions in separate PRs.

I agree with reviewers before me that many of the statements in this document are too sweeping, not (at least currently) a good fit for our codebase, and lack sufficient contributor consensus, so Approach NACK. For example, I agree with @mzumsande that continuing after a defect can be a sensible decision, especially where peers can trigger it, as we want to minimize the chances of nodes crashing. And while more consistency would be nice, I haven't converged on a single error propagation mechanism that we must always use. Both exceptions (e.g. invisible in signatures, and easy to turn into `std::terminate` from destructors or threads) and return types like `util::Expected` (e.g. boilerplate at every call site, no way to fail from a constructor) have drawbacks significant enough that I wouldn't feel comfortable mandating either.

Instead, I think it would be useful and productive to update `developer-notes.md` with the shared vocabulary (result/error/defect) outlined here, the subset of guidelines we can so far agree on (e.g. "never report an error as a negative result" seems straightforward and actionable), and specific examples of when/how it is good to throw or catch exceptions or return failure types, and when it is an anti-pattern.

As toolchains improve, our codebase evolves, and perhaps our agreement on error handling best practices increases, we can become more prescriptive over time when it makes sense.
[2026-10-07] c:6045777724 comment by purpleKarrot (member):
There are three separate points I would like to address.

1. **The meaning of “defect”**

   @stickies-v @mzumsande, I think we should be able to find common ground here, because I suspect our disagreement is primarily about terminology.

   I define a defect as an unexpected state in the program. If a function is designed to continue correctly from a particular state (even an arbitrary state) then that state is, **by definition**, accounted for by its design. It is therefore not unexpected, and hence **not a defect** in the sense I am using here.

   Under that definition, your examples of safe continuation seem compatible with my position. Can we agree on that distinction? I think making it explicit would help us avoid arguing past each other.

2. **The purpose of coding guidelines**

   I do not think coding guidelines need to describe the status quo. They can define a goal toward which the codebase should evolve. Consequently, the fact that existing code follows a different approach is not an argument against the proposed guidelines.

   The current codebase is relevant to how we implement a transition, but it does not determine whether the proposed goal is the right one. I would like us to assess that goal on its technical merits.

3. **Error propagation through consensus code**

   In my view, a stateless, side-effect-free validation library, as proposed in #35904, written in idiomatic C++ should be **free of explicit error handling code**. It should neither `throw` nor `catch`, nor wrap or unwrap runtime errors in a result type. Errors should not be stored in global variables, and functions should **not be able to intercept error propagation**.

   This last requirement goes beyond prohibiting `catch`: intermediate functions should not receive errors as values or through shared state that they can inspect, suppress, or turn into validation results. The absence of explicit error handling is a deliberate design constraint. Each such handling point creates an opportunity for misuse.

   The [2013 chain split](https://bips.dev/50/), where a database resource limit effectively became a consensus rule, is a concrete reason to take this seriously. A failure to complete validation must remain distinct from a completed validation that finds a block invalid.

   Consensus code should therefore be written so that runtime errors reported by coin lookup can safely propagate without causing damage along the way. In other words, it should conform to exception-correct programming practices. I consider this a stronger design because it removes opportunities to mishandle runtime failures from the consensus logic itself.

 I hope we can resolve the first point by agreeing on the terminology. On the other two, I recognize that we may still disagree about the design we should pursue. My position remains that guidelines should establish that goal, and that keeping explicit error handling out of consensus logic is the stronger design. I would welcome concrete technical arguments against that goal, independently of how much work it would take to reach it.
